# driftlet: a guide for agents

driftlet is a dependency-free JavaScript library that solves 1D drift–diffusion–reaction
(Poisson–Nernst–Planck) problems fast enough for live web demos. Semiconductor junctions, solar
cells, electrochemical cells, batteries, membranes and nerves are one problem with different
casts of species (electrons, holes, ions, neutral molecules), each moving down its own
electrochemical potential μ̄, coupled by Poisson's equation, reactions and interfaces. So a
device in any field is built the same way, from the same pieces. It runs in a browser, a Web
Worker or Node, from npm or a CDN.

Every code block below runs in the test suite and prints its closed-form check. Skim the next
two sections, then go to the template nearest your device:

- semiconductors: a pn junction (with an I–V sweep), a live page with a slider, a solar cell, a
  MOS capacitor, a pulse drifting along a bar (under Transients);
- electrochemistry: a cell, an electrode in a stirred solution (a potential step, and a cyclic
  voltammogram), a battery particle discharging;
- physiology: a cell membrane (a resting potential).

More in docs/templates.md: a Schottky diode, a thin-film transistor, corrosion under a drop (an
electrode spread through a film), a voltage clamp, an action potential, one travelling along an
axon.

The references are in docs/: device.md (the definition), kit.md (the helpers), conventions.md
(signs and levels), visualization.md, alignment.md (band offsets), statistics.md (non-ideal
materials, insertion hosts), data.md and reliability.md (what's validated, and the limits).

## Imports

From a CDN, pin the version you tested against:

```js nocheck
import { Device, units } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/driftlet@1.2.5/src/index.js';
import { build, layer, ohmic, semiconductor, live } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/driftlet@1.2.5/src/kit.js';
import { bandDiagram } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/driftlet@1.2.5/src/plot.js';
```

From npm: `driftlet`, `driftlet/kit`, `driftlet/plot`. Every export is listed at the end.

## What to know first

- **Units are SI**: m, mol/m³ (1 M = 1000 mol/m³; 1e16 cm⁻³ is only 0.0166 mol/m³), J/mol, m²/s,
  V, A/m², F/m², S/m². `units` converts in (`units.um(1)`, `units.perCm3(1e17)` for per cm³ or
  per cm³·s, `units.eV(1.12)` to J/mol, `units.cm2PerS(36)`, `units.molar(0.1)`) and back
  (`units.toPerCm3`, `toEV`, `toMolar`, `toUm`, …). Physiology: 1 mS/cm² = 10 S/m², 1 µF/cm² =
  0.01 F/m², 1 µA/cm² = 0.01 A/m², mM = mol/m³.
- **Everything you set or read is an electrochemical potential μ̄** (or a voltage made from one). A
  terminal's `V` is the level of its terminal species (`terminal`, which the kit's contacts set):
  for an electron contact V = −μ̄_e/F, what a voltmeter reads. φ is bookkeeping, per material, and
  never a control.
- **Solutions** are plain objects of `Float64Array`s: `x`, `phi`, and per species `c`, `mu` (μ̄),
  `V` (the species voltage μ̄/(zF): a quasi-Fermi level for e⁻ and h⁺) and `Vstd` (the standard
  level: a band edge; in volts, E = −V, so E_c is the lower line). `NaN` marks a value
  that doesn't exist (a species absent from a material, `V` of a neutral one, `c` in a metal).
- **Currents.** `sol.terminals[name]` gives each terminal's `{ V, current }`, its current into
  the device; a current drive `{ I }` is the same way round (electrons fed in are I < 0).
  `sol.current` is the right contact's toward +x, so a forward diode with its p side on the right
  carries a negative one (with ports, read each contact from `sol.terminals`). Everything is per
  m² of a planar device; with a `geometry` (shells, or any cross-section A(x)) it's a total.
- **What isn't defaulted**: an alignment between different materials, a φ law where a metal
  meets a dielectric, and the amount of anything a contact doesn't feed (`c0`). The error names
  the path and says what to give. (Kinetic details are defaulted: listed in docs/device.md.)
- **Check before trusting, early.** `sol.converged` must be true; read `sol.warnings`, where a
  failed solve always says why. Before comparing with theory, log `describe(def)` (kit: a summary
  that flags unit slips) and `check(dev, sol).text` (kit): each species' ledger, conservation in
  transients, a grid twice as fine (a FAIL means refine) and the species listed in reverse (a FAIL
  means a solve converged somewhere that isn't steady: compare a long advance()).

## How a device is written

- **`build({ T, library, stack, bulkReactions, ports, grid, geometry })`** (kit) reads a stack
  left to right: its first and last items are the contacts, `layer(material, length, opts)`s
  are regions (give one a `name` to refer to it), and any other object between two layers is
  the face between them. `ohmic()`, `bath()` and the like write contacts; a plain object works.
- **The library** is pieces with `species` and `materials`: `semiconductor('Si')` (Si, Ge, GaAs, at
  300 K; `semiconductor('Si', { T: 350 })` moves them, 150–500 K, for a device at that `T`),
  `aqueous(names)` (H⁺ Li⁺ Na⁺ K⁺ Ag⁺ Cu²⁺ Zn²⁺ Fe²⁺ Fe³⁺ OH⁻ Cl⁻ NO₃⁻ SO₄²⁻ in water, at 25
  °C; `{ epsr: 0 }` makes it strictly neutral, with no double layers), `metal('Ag')` (Ag Cu Au Al Zn
  Li Pt), all from `driftlet/kit`. A semiconductor's textbook numbers are in `SEMICONDUCTORS.Si`
  (`Eg` and `chi` in eV, `Nc` and `Nv` in cm⁻³, `mun` and `mup` in cm²/(V·s), `epsr`); in the
  material, `materials.Si.species['e-'].cRef` and `['h+'].cRef` are N_c and N_v in mol/m³ and
  h⁺'s `mu0` is the gap (e⁻'s is 0), so n_i = √(N_c N_v) e^(−E_g/2RT), 6.7e9 cm⁻³ for Si. The
  material carries the T its data are for (`materials.Si.T`), and a device at another T warns
  (its default is 298.15 K, so say `T: 300`). An alloy starts from a relative's entry with your
  numbers put in (docs/data.md has AlGaAs from GaAs). A species it lacks is pushed into both lists
  (`z: 0` for a neutral one): `lib.species.push({ name: 'A-', z: -1, cRef: 1000 })`,
  `lib.materials.water.species['A-'] = { D, mu0 }`. Only μ° differences within a reaction matter:
  for a redox couple μ°_red − μ°_ox = −F·E° (against SHE, the library's μ°_H⁺ being 0). An
  insulator is a material with no species: `{ species: [], materials: { SiO2: { epsr: 3.9, species:
  {} } } }`.
- **Faces.** Between two different non-metals, give an alignment, `{ dipole }` or `{ step: {
  species: 'e-', value } }` (J/mol), or `phi: 'neutral'`. `vacuumDipole(def, { material, anchor:
  'e-', offset: χ }, …)` estimates a dipole from electron affinities (Anderson's rule); it reads
  only the materials, so build with `{ dipole: 0 }`, then put its value in (docs/alignment.md). Next
  to a metal, a face takes no alignment, but needs a φ law if the other side has ε > 0: `{ phi: {
  type: 'capacitive', C }, zeroCharge }` or `phi: 'neutral'`, where `zeroCharge` is the metal's V −
  φ at its edge when the face holds no charge (a work-function difference, a potential of zero
  charge, a Schottky barrier). A face's reactions label sides: `'Li+(left) = Li+(right)'`.
- **Ports** are terminals attached sideways to a window inside a region (`from`, `to`, m from its
  left end): a source or drain, an injector, a reference electrode (`I: 0`), an electrode spread
  through a film (`reactions`, `area`), a gate along a channel or a membrane along an axon
  (`capacitance`, `gates`). A BJT's base contact is a port on a narrow window of the base,
  `{ region: 'base', from, to, V, terminal: 'h+', species: { 'h+': 'equilibrium' } }`.
- **Drives.** A terminal is held at a voltage `V`, driven by a current `I` (open circuit is
  `I: 0`), or behind a resistance `{ V, R }`; in `build()`, the same object goes where the
  voltage would (`ohmic({ I: 0 }, ['e-'])`, `ohmic({ V: 1, R: 1e3 }, ['e-'])`), and `set()` may
  switch one kind for another (`{ I: 0 }` drops a held `V`). Either can be a waveform: a table `{ t, values }`
  (piecewise linear; a step is two points at one time), or the kit's `pulse({ start, width,
  amplitude, rise, base })`, `square({ high, low, period, duty })`, `ramp({ from, to, duration,
  start })` or `triangle({ from, to, period })` (out and back each period from t = 0: a cyclic
  voltammogram, in terminal volts). `dev.set({ contacts: { right: { V } } })` changes a drive
  and keeps the state as a warm start; ports are patched by name, `{ ports: { gate: { V } } }`.
- **Reactions** are equations: `{ equation: 'e- + h+ = 0', kf: { Si: 1e8 } }`, a coefficient
  written with its space (`2 e-`). A participant that isn't a species (solid silver) is fixed by
  its μ: `fixed: { 'Ag(s)': 0 }`. A bulk reaction's forward rate is `kf · Π c_reactants`
  (mol/(m³·s)); the backward one follows from the μ°.
- **Recombination and light.** Band-to-band `e- + h+ = 0` gives a minority lifetime τ =
  1/(kf·N), N the majority density in mol/m³ (`kf: 1e8` is 0.6 µs at 1e16 cm⁻³); being
  bimolecular, as is the kit's `recombination()`, it shortens at high injection. SRH is `srh: { Si:
  { tauN, tauP } }` in place of `kf` (s), or at a face `{ equation: 'e-(left) + h+(right) = 0',
  srh: { vn, vp } }` (m/s); with τ_N ≪ τ_p it gives n-type silicon's holes a lifetime τ_p at any
  injection. `srh` carries no charge; for traps whose charge matters (dense or deep ones, trapped
  charge bending the bands), `trap(semiconductor('Si'), { density, tauN, tauP, n1, charge:
  'acceptor' })` writes the trap's two states as immobile species and returns `{ library,
  bulkReactions, c0 }` (c0 into each layer that has the trap): the same rate in steady state, its
  charge in Poisson. Light is a reaction from a reservoir (`photon = e- + h+`, uniform), or absorbed as
  it goes in, `photogeneration({ material, flux, alpha, mu: units.eV(3), from, to })`, `from` and
  `to` being x in the device (a port's window is instead m from its region's left end). To switch
  it during a run, `set()` the device's whole `bulkReactions` list, recombination included: in
  `set()`, a list replaces and an object merges (the state and the step size carry over).
- **Electrode kinetics.** A face reaction's `k0` (mol/(m²·s)) is its rate with every participant
  at cRef: i₀ = nF·k0 there, and k0 = k°·cRef for a textbook k° in m/s (1 cm/s at 1 M is
  `k0: 10`).
- **Grids** grade geometrically from `hmin` at each region's ends up to `hmax`, neighbouring cells
  differing by at most `ratio` (1.2): put `hmin` below the shortest length that matters (a Debye
  length, a depletion edge). Left out, `grid` is a coarse default for a first look; `check()`
  says whether a grid is fine enough.

`build()` is the usual way in. It writes a plain definition for `new Device()`, which some
templates below write by hand (where a port spans a region, or no stack fits):

```js
import { Device, FARADAY, GAS_CONSTANT } from 'driftlet';

// A concentration cell: 100 mM KCl against 10 mM through a gap, read by Ag/AgCl electrodes.
const D = { 'K+': 1.957e-9, 'Cl-': 2.032e-9 };
const dev = new Device({
  T: 298.15,
  species: [{ name: 'K+', z: 1, cRef: 1000 }, { name: 'Cl-', z: -1, cRef: 1000 }], // cRef: the standard state, mol/m³
  materials: { water: { epsr: 0, species: { 'K+': { D: D['K+'], mu0: -283.27e3 }, 'Cl-': { D: D['Cl-'], mu0: -131.23e3 } } } },
  regions: [{ name: 'gap', material: 'water', length: 100e-6, c0: { 'K+': 10, 'Cl-': 10 } }], // left to right
  // (interfaces: [...] would hold the faces between regions, one fewer than the regions)
  contacts: {
    left: { V: 0, bath: { c: { 'K+': 100, 'Cl-': 100 }, reference: 'Cl-' } }, // V is Cl⁻'s level: an Ag/AgCl electrode's
    right: { I: 0, bath: { c: { 'K+': 10, 'Cl-': 10 }, reference: 'Cl-' } }, // open circuit
  },
  grid: { hmin: 0.1e-6, hmax: 5e-6 },
});
const sol = dev.solve();
const tK = D['K+'] / (D['K+'] + D['Cl-']), VT = (GAS_CONSTANT * 298.15) / FARADAY;
console.log(`EMF ${(sol.terminals.right.V * 1e3).toFixed(3)} mV, 2t₊V_T ln 10 = ${(2 * tK * VT * Math.log(10) * 1e3).toFixed(3)} mV`); // 58.048, 58.047
```

An ion-exchange membrane is a layer whose material has its ions slower, with a `fixedCharge` (−X·F
for X mol/m³ of fixed anions), between layers of water. A bath against the membrane itself names
its own material, `bath(c, 'Cl-', 0, { material: 'water' })`, and meets it through a Donnan step.
An exchange or partition constant between the membrane and the water is a difference of μ°:
give the membrane's ions μ° shifted from the water's by s_i, and K = e^(−(s_Na − s_H)/RT) for
Na⁺ against H⁺ (a large K draws in salt too, unless the co-ion's s is raised). The membrane
demo's page script is a worked example.

## Template: a semiconductor junction

```js
import { Device, units } from 'driftlet';
import { build, layer, ohmic, semiconductor, describe } from 'driftlet/kit';

const def = build({
  T: 300, // the library's semiconductor data are for 300 K, unless semiconductor('Si', { T })
  library: [semiconductor('Si')],
  stack: [
    ohmic(0), // e⁻ and h⁺ in equilibrium with a metal at 0 V
    layer('Si', units.um(1), { name: 'n', donors: units.perCm3(1e17) }),
    layer('Si', units.um(1), { name: 'p', acceptors: units.perCm3(1e16) }),
    ohmic(0.5), // the p side at +0.5 V: forward bias
  ],
  // recombination: τ = 1/(kf·N) ≈ 0.6 µs at N = 1e16 cm⁻³, so L = √(Dτ) ≈ 50 µm ≫ 1 µm: a short
  // diode, whose Shockley J₀ takes each side's quasi-neutral width (W − x_d) in place of L
  bulkReactions: [{ equation: 'e- + h+ = 0', kf: { Si: 1e8 } }],
  grid: { hmin: units.nm(1), hmax: units.nm(20) },
});
console.log(describe(def));
const dev = new Device(def);
const sol = dev.solve();
console.log(sol.converged, `I = ${sol.current.toFixed(1)} A/m²`); // negative: toward −x, p to n
// An I–V sweep: change the drive, solve again (warm-started).
for (const V of [0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6]) {
  dev.set({ contacts: { right: { V } } });
  console.log(V, dev.solve().current);
}
```

## Template: a live page with a slider

`live()` warm-starts each solve, merges slider moves made during one, and keeps the last good
solution (on a failure, `info.failed` and `info.error` are set). It returns `{ set, solution, ready,
close }`; `set()` and `ready` (the first solve) are promises of `{ solution, info }`.
`bandDiagram()` returns an SVG string; a fixed `range` keeps its axis still. `worker: true` solves
in a Web Worker, from a CDN too. A few hundred nodes solve in milliseconds; thousands, or
transients, want a worker and `advance(t, { budgetMs })` per frame. `onsolution` may call `set()`,
if that converges rather than oscillates. (A headless browser screenshotting a page that loads from
a CDN needs a long virtual-time budget, 30 s.)

```html
<!doctype html>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>pn junction</title>
<label>bias <input id="V" type="range" min="-0.5" max="0.7" step="0.01" value="0"></label>
<span id="readout"></span>
<div id="figure"></div>
<script type="module">
import { units } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/driftlet@1.2.5/src/index.js';
import { build, layer, ohmic, semiconductor, live } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/driftlet@1.2.5/src/kit.js';
import { bandDiagram } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/driftlet@1.2.5/src/plot.js';

const def = build({
  T: 300,
  library: [semiconductor('Si')],
  stack: [ohmic(0), layer('Si', 1e-6, { donors: units.perCm3(1e17) }), layer('Si', 1e-6, { acceptors: units.perCm3(1e16) }), ohmic(0)],
  bulkReactions: [{ equation: 'e- + h+ = 0', kf: { Si: 1e8 } }],
  grid: { hmin: 1e-9, hmax: 20e-9 },
});
const slider = document.getElementById('V');
const dev = live(def, {
  onsolution(sol, info) {
    document.getElementById('figure').innerHTML = bandDiagram(sol, { energy: true, range: [-1.2, 1.7], title: `V = ${sol.terminals.right.V.toFixed(2)} V` });
    document.getElementById('readout').textContent = info.failed ? 'no solution here' : `I = ${sol.current.toExponential(2)} A/m²`;
  },
});
slider.addEventListener('input', () => dev.set({ contacts: { right: { V: +slider.value } } }));
</script>
```

To draw in your own style, `traces(sol, opts)` (kit, the same options) gives the lines as data;
see "Reading level diagrams" below.

For an explainer, `particles(sol, { weight, cap })` (kit) draws a solution as dots, each `weight`
mol/m² of a species, hopping at the solution's rates, so their density and net crossings agree
with it on average; say on the page that they sample the continuum solution. A cell over `cap`
dots is a sea, shaded by `expected(name)`. Each frame, `swarm.step(dt)`, then draw `swarm.dots`
and `swarm.events` (docs/kit.md; the pn, axon and membrane demos are worked examples).

## Template: a solar cell

`photon = e- + h+`, with the photons' μ well above the gap, generates uniformly at the rate `kf`.
Open circuit is `I: 0`, and the terminal's V is then V_oc. The photocurrent flows toward +x
(holes to the p side, on the right), so the power the cell delivers is V·`sol.current`. Light
absorbed as it goes in, for a cell's thickness to matter, is `photogeneration()` (above).

```js
import { Device, units } from 'driftlet';
import { build, layer, ohmic, semiconductor } from 'driftlet/kit';

const cell = (right) =>
  build({
    T: 300,
    library: [semiconductor('Si')],
    stack: [
      ohmic(0),
      layer('Si', units.um(1), { name: 'n', donors: units.perCm3(1e18) }),
      layer('Si', units.um(100), { name: 'p', acceptors: units.perCm3(1e16) }),
      ohmic(right),
    ],
    bulkReactions: [
      { equation: 'e- + h+ = 0', kf: { Si: 1e8 } }, // τ ≈ 0.6 µs in the p base: L ≈ 48 µm
      { equation: 'photon = e- + h+', fixed: { photon: units.eV(3) }, kf: { Si: 50 } }, // G, mol/(m³·s)
    ],
    grid: { hmin: units.nm(1), hmax: units.um(1) },
  });
const sc = new Device(cell(0)).solve(); // short circuit
const oc = new Device(cell({ I: 0 })).solve(); // open circuit
console.log(`J_sc = ${sc.current.toFixed(1)} A/m², V_oc = ${oc.terminals.right.V.toFixed(3)} V`);
```

In an organic cell, light makes excitons, a neutral species made by `photogeneration({ ...,
makes: 'X' })`, which split at the donor/acceptor face by a reaction, `X = h+(left) + e-(right)`
(e⁻ and h⁺ blocked there; the face's `step` sets E_CT). The organic demo's page script is a
worked example, checked against exciton diffusion and detailed balance.

For a perovskite cell, prefer the curated `perovskiteCell({ V, light, bulkSRH })`: IonMonger's
default cell (mobile iodide vacancies), with its J–V scans at seven rates in `PEROVSKITE_SCANS`
and `hysteresis(trace, turn)` to read the same figures from yours.

## Template: a MOS capacitor

The gate is a metal layer with a capacitive face to the oxide (a metal screens within Å, so C is
large) and the gate's alignment as `zeroCharge`. In 1D nothing supplies the inversion layer's
electrons (a MOSFET's source and drain do), so a port holds their level at the surface: the
low-frequency C–V. The gate's charge is the displacement into the oxide, `sol.interfaces[0].D`.

```js
import { Device, units, EPS0, FARADAY, GAS_CONSTANT } from 'driftlet';
import { build, layer, ohmic, semiconductor, metal, vacuumZeroCharge } from 'driftlet/kit';

const oxide = { species: [], materials: { SiO2: { epsr: 3.9, species: {} } } };
const tox = units.nm(10), Cox = (3.9 * EPS0) / tox, NA = units.perCm3(1e17);
const mos = (Vg, zeroCharge) =>
  build({
    T: 300,
    library: [semiconductor('Si'), metal('Al'), oxide],
    stack: [
      ohmic(Vg, ['e-']), // the gate's terminal: the aluminium's electrons
      layer('Al', units.nm(20)),
      { phi: { type: 'capacitive', C: 10 }, zeroCharge }, // the gate's face
      layer('SiO2', tox),
      { dipole: 0 }, // the oxide holds no species, so this alignment changes nothing
      layer('Si', units.um(1), { name: 'Si', acceptors: NA }),
      ohmic(0),
    ],
    ports: [{ name: 'channel', region: 'Si', from: 0, to: units.nm(1), V: 0, terminal: 'e-', species: { 'e-': 'equilibrium' } }],
    grid: { hmin: units.nm(0.25), hmax: units.nm(50), ratio: 1.15 },
  });
// The gate's alignment from vacuum levels: Al's work function 4.1 eV, Si's electron affinity 4.05 eV.
const zc = vacuumZeroCharge(mos(0, 0), 4.1, { material: 'Si', anchor: 'e-', offset: 4.05 });
const dev = new Device(mos(0, zc));
const Q = (Vg) => {
  dev.set({ contacts: { left: { V: Vg } } });
  return dev.solve().interfaces[0].D;
};
for (const Vg of [-2, -0.95, 0, 0.4, 2]) {
  const C = (Q(Vg + 0.01) - Q(Vg - 0.01)) / 0.02;
  console.log(`V_G ${Vg} V: C/C_ox ${(C / Cox).toFixed(3)}`); // 0.949, 0.701 (flat band), 0.267, 0.375, 0.973
}
// At flat band the silicon is a capacitor of ε/L_D, its Debye length's.
const LD = Math.sqrt((11.9 * EPS0 * GAS_CONSTANT * 300) / (FARADAY * FARADAY * NA)); // (the kit's Si: ε 11.9)
console.log(`flat band, theory: ${(1 / (1 + (Cox * LD) / (11.9 * EPS0))).toFixed(3)}`); // 0.701
```

`dev.impedance([f], { terminal: 'left' })` (C = Im(1/Z)/ω, from `{ f, Z: { re, im } }`) gives
the same C at any frequency with the port; without it, only below the minority supply's knee
(generation, or diffusion from the back contact: 0.01 Hz and below), and the high-frequency C–V
above. Draw it with
`bandDiagram(sol, { energy: true, phi: ['SiO2'] })`: across an insulator φ is the line to draw.

## Template: an electrochemical cell

An electrode is a metal layer with the reaction at its face, behind a contact holding the
metal's electrons (`ohmic(V, ['e-'])`).

```js
import { Device } from 'driftlet';
import { build, layer, ohmic, half, level, SHE, aqueous, metal } from 'driftlet/kit';

const silver = half('Ag+ + e- = Ag(s)', { 'Ag(s)': 0 }); // μ of the element: 0 on table conventions
// A Stern layer at each metal face: its capacitance and the potential of zero charge are
// properties of that interface, so they're yours to choose.
const face = { phi: { type: 'capacitive', C: 0.2 }, zeroCharge: 0.1, reactions: [{ ...silver, k0: 1e-3, alpha: 0.5 }] };
const def = build({
  library: [aqueous(['H+', 'Ag+', 'NO3-']), metal('Ag')],
  stack: [
    ohmic(0, ['e-']),
    layer('Ag', 1e-6),
    face,
    layer('water', 20e-6, { c0: { 'H+': 1, 'Ag+': 10, 'NO3-': 11 } }),
    face,
    layer('Ag', 1e-6),
    ohmic(0.05, ['e-']),
  ],
  grid: { hmin: 0.1e-9, hmax: 200e-9, ratio: 1.15 },
});
const sol = new Device(def).solve();
const mid = sol.x.length >> 1;
console.log(`I = ${sol.current.toFixed(2)} A/m²`);
// The silver couple's redox level, and the SHE level, mid-cell (electron voltages).
console.log(level(sol, silver)[mid] - level(sol, SHE, { standard: true })[mid]); // ≈ 0.80 + (RT/F) ln(c/1 M)
```

## Template: an electrode in a stirred solution, and a potential step

A working electrode, a stagnant layer, and the stirred bulk as a bath whose terminal is its
reference species (Cl⁻: an Ag/AgCl reference). An electrode's potential against SHE is its
electrons' V minus φ in the bulk (with the library's μ°), and a Cl⁻ terminal sits ~1.36 V above
that, so an electrode held at 0 V beside it is strongly anodic: `describe(def)` says where SHE
sits, and an offset of that much (`bath(c, 'Cl-', 0, { offset })`) makes the terminal read SHE.
The working electrode's current is positive when oxidising. The layer's resistance is in series
(uncompensated IR: keep it thin, or the supporting salt strong); a 100:1 excess of salt still
leaves the limiting current about 1% off pure diffusion.

```js
import { Device, GAS_CONSTANT, FARADAY } from 'driftlet';
import { build, layer, ohmic, bath, half, aqueous, metal, IONS } from 'driftlet/kit';

const iron = half('Fe3+ + e- = Fe2+');
const electrode = (drive) =>
  build({
    library: [aqueous(['K+', 'Cl-', 'Fe3+', 'Fe2+'], { epsr: 0 }), metal('Pt')],
    stack: [
      ohmic(drive, ['e-']), // the working electrode's terminal: the platinum's electrons
      layer('Pt', 1e-6),
      { reactions: [{ ...iron, k0: 1e-3 }] }, // i₀ = F·k0 ≈ 96 A/m² at 1 M each; about 1 A/m² at these mM
      layer('water', 20e-6), // the stagnant layer
      bath({ 'K+': 500, 'Cl-': 535, 'Fe3+': 5, 'Fe2+': 10 }, 'Cl-'), // the stirred bulk (neutral)
    ],
    grid: { hmin: 10e-9, hmax: 0.5e-6 },
  });
// At rest (no current), the electrode sits at the couple's Nernst potential.
const rest = new Device(electrode({ I: 0 })).solve();
const vsSHE = (sol) => sol.V['e-'][0] - sol.phi.at(-1);
const VT = (GAS_CONSTANT * 298.15) / FARADAY, Erest = vsSHE(rest);
console.log(`rest ${Erest.toFixed(4)} V vs SHE; E° + V_T ln(c₃/c₂) = ${(0.769 + VT * Math.log(5 / 10)).toFixed(4)} V`);
const drive = (E) => E - Erest + rest.terminals.left.V; // the terminal voltage for E vs SHE
// Steady, 0.2 V positive of rest: oxidising Fe²⁺. Its limiting current F·D·c/L is 35 A/m²; the
// kinetics (i₀ ≈ 1 A/m²) still hold it to about half here.
console.log(`anodic ${new Device(electrode(drive(Erest + 0.2))).solve().terminals.left.current.toFixed(2)} A/m²`); // 16.81
// A potential step from rest to 0.5 V positive: at first Fe²⁺ is depleted as at a plane,
// Cottrell's F·c·√(D/πt), until the stagnant layer is crossed (L²/D ≈ 0.5 s).
const dev = new Device(electrode(drive(Erest)));
dev.solve();
dev.set({ contacts: { left: { V: drive(Erest + 0.5) } } });
const run = dev.advance(0.03, { dtMax: 1e-3 }); // run.trace: this call's accepted steps
for (const t of [3e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2]) {
  const k = run.trace.t.findIndex((tk) => tk >= t);
  // (trace.current is the right contact's toward +x: positive for an anodic electrode on the left)
  console.log(`${t * 1e3} ms: ${run.trace.current[k].toFixed(2)} A/m², Cottrell ${(FARADAY * 10 * Math.sqrt(IONS['Fe2+'].D / (Math.PI * run.trace.t[k]))).toFixed(2)}`);
}
```

A cyclic voltammogram is this electrode driven by `triangle({ from, to, period })`, the period
being 2|to − from| over the scan rate: `solve()` it at `from` first, since the scan starts there
at t = 0, then `advance()` with a `dtMax` of a millivolt's worth of sweep, or the trace's points
fall a few mV apart and miss the peaks. For a diffusion peak (Randles–Ševčík), the stagnant layer
must be well past √(D·t_scan), a few hundred µm: the template's 20 µm gives a thin-layer wave.
Its potential against the bath's terminal is −`trace.voltage` (that is V_right − V_left), and
`trace.current` is anodic positive.

## Template: a battery particle discharging

A battery's insertion electrode is a material described by its OCV curve (docs/statistics.md):
here one particle of a cathode, a sphere, the single-particle model. Li⁺ is held at its surface
by the electrolyte, and the electrons come in through a port there (a current into the device,
so negative to discharge a cathode). With no steady state while a current flows, it's `advance()`d
from its `c0`, never `solve()`d. `D` is the dilute value: an ideal host's chemical diffusivity is
D/(1 − x), so it fills more easily the fuller it gets. A real OCV curve with a plateau needs a
little of the ideal slope (the error says how much).

```js
import { Device, FARADAY, GAS_CONSTANT } from 'driftlet';

const T = 298.15, VT = (GAS_CONSTANT * T) / FARADAY;
const R = 5e-6, D = 1e-14, cMax = 50000, x0 = 0.1; // m, m²/s, mol/m³ of sites, starting fill
const xs = Array.from({ length: 99 }, (_, k) => (k + 1) / 100);
const particle = (I) =>
  new Device({
    T,
    species: [{ name: 'Li+', z: 1 }, { name: 'e-', z: -1 }],
    materials: {
      host: {
        epsr: 0,
        species: { 'Li+': { D, mu0: 0, cRef: cMax }, 'e-': { D: 1e-4, mu0: 0, cRef: cMax } },
        statistics: [{ type: 'insertion', species: ['Li+', 'e-'], cMax, ocv: { x: xs, E: xs.map((x) => 4 - VT * Math.log(x / (1 - x))), muRef: 0 } }],
      },
    },
    geometry: { type: 'spherical', r0: 0 }, // x is the radius; currents are totals (A)
    regions: [{ name: 'p', material: 'host', length: R, c0: { 'Li+': x0 * cMax, 'e-': x0 * cMax } }],
    contacts: {
      left: { phi: 'neutral' }, // the centre
      right: { V: 0, terminal: 'Li+', species: { 'Li+': 'equilibrium' }, phi: 'bulk' }, // Li⁺ at the electrolyte's level
    },
    ports: [{ name: 'wire', region: 'p', from: 0.98 * R, to: R, I, terminal: 'e-', species: { 'e-': { type: 'conductance', G: 1e15 } } }],
    grid: { hmin: R / 400, hmax: R / 40 },
  });
const Q = FARADAY * cMax * (4 / 3) * Math.PI * R ** 3; // C for Δx = 1
const xEnd = 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-0.1 / VT)); // the OCV reaches a 3.9 V cutoff at x = 0.98
for (const C of [0.2, 20]) {
  const I = -(C * (xEnd - x0) * Q) / 3600; // a C-rate: the whole window in 1/C hours
  const dev = particle(I);
  // Halfway: in u = −ln(1 − x), whose diffusivity is D however full, a constant flux q in makes a
  // quasi-steady parabola, surface − centre = qR/(2D c_max), once t ≫ R²/(π²D) (250 s here).
  const half = dev.advance(1800 / C), u = (c) => -Math.log(1 - c / cMax), q = -I / (FARADAY * 4 * Math.PI * R * R);
  const du = u(half.c['Li+'].at(-1)) - u(half.c['Li+'][0]);
  let sol = half;
  while (sol.converged && sol.terminals.wire.V > 3.9) sol = dev.advance(sol.time + 36 / C); // on to the cutoff, in 1% steps
  console.log(`${C}C: ${((100 * (-I * sol.time)) / Q / (xEnd - x0)).toFixed(0)}% of the capacity; halfway, Δu ${du.toFixed(4)}, qR/(2D c_max) ${((q * R) / (2 * D * cMax)).toFixed(4)}`);
} // 0.2C: 100%, 0.0205 against 0.0204; 20C: 91%, and halfway (90 s) is too soon for the parabola
```

## Template: a cell membrane

A lipid bilayer is a face: a capacitor (1 µF/cm², 0.01 F/m²) crossed by channels with a
permeability (`{ type: 'permeability', P }`, m/s: Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz comes out of it) and by
pumps, reactions with saturating kinetics (`vmax`, `K`). The membrane potential is φ_in − φ_out,
read from `sol.phi` as below. (A bath's terminal V is its φ only without a reference species,
`bath(c, drive)`; `bath(c, 'Cl-')`'s is Cl⁻'s level, which differs by Cl⁻'s Nernst term.)

```js
import { Device, FARADAY, GAS_CONSTANT } from 'driftlet';
import { build, layer, bath, aqueous, check } from 'driftlet/kit';

const T = 310.15, VT = (GAS_CONSTANT * T) / FARADAY;
const out = { 'Na+': 145, 'K+': 5, 'Cl-': 110, 'A-': 40 }; // mM = mol/m³; A⁻: anions that don't cross
const inside = { 'Na+': 12, 'K+': 140, 'Cl-': 10, 'A-': 142 };
const water = aqueous(['Na+', 'K+', 'Cl-'], { epsr: 0 }); // strictly neutral solutions
water.species.push({ name: 'A-', z: -1, cRef: 1000 });
water.materials.water.species['A-'] = { D: 0.5e-9, mu0: 0 };
const P = { 'K+': 1e-8, 'Na+': 0.04e-8, 'Cl-': 0.45e-8 }; // m/s, Hodgkin and Katz's ratios
const membrane = {
  phi: { type: 'capacitive', C: 0.01 },
  species: { 'K+': { type: 'permeability', P: P['K+'] }, 'Na+': { type: 'permeability', P: P['Na+'] }, 'Cl-': { type: 'permeability', P: P['Cl-'] }, 'A-': 'blocked' },
  // The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (outside on the left): 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, per ATP (50 kJ/mol); vmax ≈ 3000
  // pumps per µm² at 100 cycles/s.
  reactions: [{ equation: '3 Na+(right) + 2 K+(left) + ATP = 3 Na+(left) + 2 K+(right) + ADP', fixed: { ATP: 50e3, ADP: 0 }, vmax: 5e-7, K: { 'Na+': 10, 'K+': 1.5 } }],
};
const cell = build({
  T,
  library: [water],
  stack: [
    bath(out, 'Cl-'), // the extracellular fluid, held
    layer('water', 1e-6, { name: 'outside', c0: out }),
    membrane,
    layer('water', 5e-6, { name: 'cytoplasm', c0: inside }), // a closed cell: its contents set by leaks and the pump
    { species: { 'Na+': 'blocked', 'K+': 'blocked', 'Cl-': 'blocked', 'A-': 'blocked' }, phi: 'neutral' },
  ],
  grid: { hmin: 50e-9, hmax: 200e-9 },
});
const dev = new Device(cell), sol = dev.solve();
const g = sol.x.length - 1, ci = (s) => sol.c[s][g], Vm = sol.phi[g] - sol.phi[0];
// Mullins–Noda: in steady state the pump's 3:2 sets the ratio of the Na⁺ and K⁺ leaks.
const mn = VT * Math.log((1.5 * P['K+'] * out['K+'] + P['Na+'] * out['Na+']) / (1.5 * P['K+'] * ci('K+') + P['Na+'] * ci('Na+')));
console.log(`V_m = ${(Vm * 1e3).toFixed(2)} mV (Mullins–Noda ${(mn * 1e3).toFixed(2)}), inside Na⁺ ${ci('Na+').toFixed(1)} K⁺ ${ci('K+').toFixed(1)} mM`);
console.log(check(dev, sol).text); // per compartment: Na⁺ leaks into the cytoplasm as fast as it's pumped out
```

Between two baths instead (the inside one `bath(inside, 'Cl-', { I: 0 })`: held composition, no
current), V_m is GHK. Without the pump, a closed cell runs down to Donnan equilibrium.

## Transients

`advance(t, opts)` steps adaptively from the device's present state (its `c0`, or the steady
state if you called `solve()`) to time t, absolute (for a further dt, `advance(sol.time + dt)`). It returns the solution there, with `done` and a `trace`
of this call's accepted steps (`t`, `current`, `voltage`: V_right − V_left). It stops short at
`budgetMs` (an animation frame: call again) or, with a warning saying why, at `maxSteps` (100000)
or a step that won't converge. `probes`, read at accepted steps (give `dtMax` to resolve them):
`{ x, species }` (c, or `quantity: 'V'`), `{ x, quantity: 'phi' }`, and at a face `{ interface: f,
species }` (its flux) or `{ interface: f, gate }`.

- **Events.** To stop at one (a cut-off voltage, a diode's storage time), advance in short calls
  and test after each: a driven current held past what the device can pass fails to converge.
- **The first instants.** The first step is sized by error control (from 1e-4 of the interval),
  so a fast start (an initial plateau, a charging spike) can fall inside it: give `dt0` (and
  `dtMax`) to see it. A voltage step's first point carries the displacement that charges the bulk
  at once (a spike of ~1e4 A/m² for ~1e-10 s across a cell's Stern layers): leave it out of
  integrals of I²R.
- **Storage.** A device that only stores what comes in (a battery host filling at a current, a
  gate charging) has no steady state: `advance()` it from its `c0`, don't `solve()` it
  (docs/statistics.md). At no current (`I: 0`), `solve()` keeps the charge it holds: a closed
  battery sits at the OCV of its state of charge, a floating gate keeps its charge.
- **Other steps.** `dev.step(dt)` is one backward-Euler step, and `dev.impedance(frequencies,
  { terminal })` the small-signal Z(f) about the steady state, in Ω·m².

```js
import { Device, units, FARADAY } from 'driftlet';
import { build, layer, ohmic, semiconductor, pulse, injector, recombination } from 'driftlet/kit';

// A pulse of holes injected into an n-type germanium bar under a field (Haynes–Shockley), and
// the hole density read 1 mm downstream as it drifts past.
const L = 4e-3, ND = units.perCm3(1e15), E = 1000; // m, mol/m³, V/m (10 V/cm)
const width = 0.5e-6, I = (0.05 * ND * FARADAY * 50e-6) / width; // s; A/m²: 5% of n₀ over 50 µm
const def = build({
  T: 300,
  library: [semiconductor('Ge')],
  stack: [ohmic(E * L), layer('Ge', L, { name: 'bar', donors: ND }), ohmic(0)], // holes drift toward +x
  bulkReactions: [recombination({ material: 'Ge', tau: 20e-6, majority: ND })], // the minority lifetime
  ports: [injector({ region: 'bar', from: 0.5e-3, to: 0.55e-3, species: 'h+', I: pulse({ width, amplitude: I, rise: 1e-9 }) })],
  grid: { hmin: units.um(10), hmax: units.um(10) },
});
const dev = new Device(def);
const rest = dev.solve(); // the steady state at t = 0 (solve() doesn't advance time)
const run = dev.advance(10e-6, { dtMax: 20e-9, probes: [{ x: 1.525e-3, species: 'h+' }] });
const seen = run.trace.probes[0], k = seen.indexOf(Math.max(...seen));
const tArrive = run.trace.t[k] - width / 2; // from the pulse's middle
console.log(`peak at ${(run.trace.t[k] * 1e6).toFixed(2)} µs, Δp ${units.toPerCm3(seen[k] - rest.c['h+'][0]).toExponential(1)} cm⁻³: μ_p ≈ ${(1e-3 / (E * tArrive) * 1e4).toFixed(0)} cm²/(V·s)`); // ≈ 1950 for the 1900 put in: a spreading, decaying pulse peaks a little early
```

To start from a state rather than simulate how it got there (a packet already injected, a salt
gradient laid down), give a region's `c0` a profile, `{ 'h+': { x: [...], values: [...] } }` against
the device's x, and `advance()` the new `Device` without `solve()`. A given `c0` is the starting
state even for a species a contact feeds; the rest start at their contact's level. The grid isn't
fitted to the profile: grade it fine where the profile is steep (a warning says where it isn't).
`advance()`'s `tol` (1e-3) is each step's error, in thermal units: tighten it, or cap `dtMax`, for
numbers to compare with theory.

Transients cost more where a carrier's density spans many decades (minority holes in silicon)
and at strong injection; budget for that, or coarsen the grid. `recorder(dev, { every, times,
probes })` (kit) runs one in pieces: `rec.trace` is the whole run's, and `rec.frame(t)` the
whole solution at or before t, for a time slider.

## Reading level diagrams

What `bandDiagram()` and `traces()` draw, and how to explain it (docs/visualization.md has more):

- **Which picture.** For electrons and holes only, draw the familiar band diagram, energy up:
  `bandDiagram(sol, { energy: true })` (E_c, E_v, E_Fn, E_Fp in eV, E = −V). The species voltages
  below are the same lines in volts, turned over: use them where ions share the diagram, or for
  equilibrium between species, never in place of the band diagram.
- **Species voltage** V_i = μ̄_i/(z_iF) (thick, solid): the Fermi level for e⁻ (what a voltmeter
  reads), a quasi-Fermi level in a semiconductor, what a reversible electrode reads for an ion.
  Each species moves down its own μ̄_i, drift and diffusion together, so its current flows down
  slopes in V_i (cations and holes downhill, electrons and anions uphill); flat is equilibrium,
  and a step at a face is resistance there. Call it the species voltage and say what it is, since
  it's new to most readers; credit Jamnik and Maier (Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. 3, 1668 (2001))
  where V_i rails explain impedance or linear response.
- **Standard level** V°_i = φ + μ°_i/(z_iF) (thin, solid): a band edge for e⁻ and h⁺; V_i − V°_i =
  (RT/z_iF) ln(c/c_ref) for ideal species. Its steps at faces are bookkeeping.
- **Redox level** of Ox + z e⁻ ⇌ Red (`level(sol, half)`, or `levels: [{ half }]` in the plot
  options; thick, dashed): (μ̄_Ox − μ̄_Red)/(zF), where an electrode by that couple would sit in
  equilibrium with the local solution. At an electrode its step from the metal's Fermi level is
  the surface overpotential. `standard: true` gives its standard level (thin, dashed).
- **Electrode potentials** are gaps to the SHE's standard level, which with the library's μ° is φ
  in water (`phi: true` draws it): E = V_e⁻(electrode) − V°_e⁻(SHE).
- **What's left out.** φ is a per-material convention, and −eφ isn't any electron's energy, so it
  isn't drawn, except across an insulator with no mobile species (`phi: ['SiO2']`: its slope is
  the field). No level is a fixed reference: shifting every line together changes nothing. A gap
  between two species' levels carries the elements' conventional zeros, so read it through a
  reaction; `shifts` (marked ⌇) moves one species' lines to fit a shared axis.
- **Your own style.** `traces(sol, opts)` gives `{ x, series: [{ id, label, kind, role, slot, y }],
  regions, faces, range }`: `kind` says how a line reads (`'level'`, `'standard'`, `'redox'`,
  `'redox-standard'`, `'phi'`; an `id` is the kind and species, `V:e-`, `Vstd:h+`), `themeColor(role,
  slot)` (plot) gives our colours,
  `labelParts(label)` splits TeX-style subscripts, `NaN` breaks a line, and a face's doubled nodes
  share an x (a vertical step).

## Good habits

- **Draw the closed-form answer alongside the simulation** wherever a textbook limit exists, as
  the templates do. A solver's output looks authoritative even when an input is wrong, and a
  mismatch is the cheapest way to catch it. Where the two should differ, say why.
- **Stay honestly inside 1D.** Where the real device isn't one-dimensional, say so and pick the
  slice that tells the true story: a MOSFET as its gate stack or its channel, never both (pinch-off
  is 2D); a BJT along its emitter–base–collector axis; one particle of a porous battery electrode
  rather than the whole electrode (that's a P2D model).

## Common mistakes

Errors say what to give, and a misspelt option is an error that names the one meant. Beyond
those:

- **A gate as a contact on an oxide.** It fails as `'e-' is absent from the end material 'SiO2'`: make the
  gate a metal layer with a capacitive face, as in the MOS template.
- **Ions on both sides of a reacting face.** Label them, `'Li+(left) = Li+(right)'`, and block
  them (`species: { 'Li+': 'blocked' }`) if they cross only by the reaction.
- **Unit slips.** D in cm²/s, μ° in eV, µF/cm², mS/cm², T in °C. `describe(def)` flags them.
- **A couple's μ° with the wrong sign** solves happily at −E° for +E°: μ°_red − μ°_ox = −F·E°.
  Check the rest potential against E°, as the stirred-solution template does.
- **The library's data are for 25 °C** (its semiconductors for 300 K: give `T: 300`, or the
  same `T` to `semiconductor(name, { T })`, which moves the gap, N_c, N_v and the mobilities; a
  mismatch warns). On a live device change both at once, `dev.set({ T, materials:
  semiconductor('Si', { T }).materials })`. A diode's J₀ ∝ T^(4−γ) e^(−E_g/kT), so its Arrhenius
  slope is E_g − T dE_g/dT + (4−γ)kT (≈ 1.24 eV for Si), not E_g. Hot and lightly doped, n_i
  passes the doping (Ge 6e15 cm⁻³ at 450 K) and the junction fades: compare before fitting V(T).
  At body temperature the same μ° and D are a fair start; D rises about 2% per kelvin in water.
- **A steady solve of a closed cell where every ion can cross**: its steady state is complete
  mixing. To watch a junction or a salt bridge, `advance()` from the unmixed `c0`.
- **A sharp junction between very different solutions** (3 M KCl against 1 µM) can't start:
  grade it over a few thin layers, as at a frit.
- **Changing `c0` with `set()`.** A carried state keeps what it holds: make a new `Device`.
- **A charged electrode face beside a strictly neutral solution** (`epsr: 0`, a capacitive face
  with reactions): refining the grid there makes the kinetics worse, not better, since the edge
  cell holds the double layer's charge. Read `sol.warnings`; a `zeroCharge` near the rest
  potential avoids it.
- **An unresolved double layer.** If `sol.warnings` says so, refine the grid (`hmin` below the
  Debye length) or use a neutral model (`epsr: 0`, `phi: 'neutral'`).

## Exports

- `driftlet`: `Device`, `units`, `DeviceError`, `SolverError`, and the constants `FARADAY`,
  `GAS_CONSTANT`, `EPS0`, `BOLTZMANN`, `ELEMENTARY_CHARGE`, `AVOGADRO` (there's no thermal-voltage
  constant: V_T = GAS_CONSTANT·T/FARADAY).
- `driftlet/kit`:
  - building: `build`, `combine`, `layer`, `ohmic`, `bath`, `half`, `level`, `SHE`,
    `vacuumLevel`, `vacuumDipole`, `vacuumZeroCharge`, and the data library (`aqueous`,
    `semiconductor`, `metal`, `trap`, `IONS`, `SEMICONDUCTORS`, `METALS`, `H2O`, `WATER_EPSR`);
  - sources: `pulse`, `square`, `triangle`, `ramp`, `injector`, `recombination`,
    `photogeneration`;
  - channels: `hodgkinHuxley`, `ghkCurrent`;
  - checking: `describe`, `unitWarnings` (describe's unit slips alone), `check`, `polarization` (an electrode's reactions at hypothetical
    metal levels, with the solution held: an Evans diagram), `henderson` and `planck`
    (liquid-junction potentials);
  - pages: `live`, `traces` (with `speciesRole` and `typeset` for its labels), `recorder`,
    `particles`;
  - curated devices: `perovskiteCell`, `PEROVSKITE_SCANS`, `hysteresis`.
- `driftlet/plot` (a quick look): `bandDiagram`, `levelChart`, `labelParts`, `themeColor`,
  `THEME`. These draw profiles in x; an I–V curve or a transient you draw yourself.
